Part 1: Theoretical Foundations of Tidy Data

Data science workflows rarely begin with clean, ready-to-analyze data. Real-world datasets often arrive in arbitrary, humanreadable layouts designed for printing, manual entry, or legacy reporting databases rather than statistical computation. To bridge the gap between raw data ingestion and analytical modeling, the data science ecosystem relies heavily on the Tidy Data framework, codified by Hadley Wickham.

1.1 The Anatomy of Tidy Data

A dataset is a collection of values (numbers or strings). Every value belongs to a variable and an observation.

  • Variable: An attribute that measures the same underlying characteristic (e.g., height, temperature, age, income) across multiple entities.
  • Observation: A set of measurements taken under similar conditions (e.g., a specific person at a specific time, a country in a specific year, a meteorological station during a given hour).

When these elements are mapped onto a rectangular data frame (such as a tibble or data frame in R), tidy data enforces three strict, interdependent criteria:

Each variable forms a column. If a dataset tracks height, weight, and age, there must be exactly three primary data columns: height, weight, and age.

Each observation forms a row. If a dataset tracks 50 unique clinical trial participants measured at baseline, there must be exactly 50 rows (assuming one row per participant).

Each value forms a cell. Every intersection of a row and a column contains a single, atomic value. Cells must not contain nested lists, multiple delimited tokens packed into a single string (unless explicitly parsed), or compound objects that require split operations during calculation.

+------------------------------------------------------+ TIDY | STRUCTURE |

+---------------------------------

----------------------+

| Observation 1 -> [ Cell ] [ Cell ] [ Cell ] (Vars) | | Observation 2 -> [ Cell ] [ Cell ] [ Cell ] | | Observation 3 -> [ Cell ] [ Cell ] [ Cell ] |

+---------------------------------

----------------------+

1.2 Why Tidy Data Matters

When data adheres to these principles, it forms a consistent contract with your data manipulation and visualization pipelines:

  • Vectorized Operations: Functions in packages like dplyr and ggplot2 assume that columns represent independent variables. This allows operations to occur vector-wise across entire columns without manual looping.
  • Grammar of Graphics Harmony: ggplot2 maps variables directly to visual aesthetics (e.g., aes(x = year, y = gdp, color = country)). If your dataset stores years as column headers and country-years as cell intersections, mapping aesthetics becomes mathematically cumbersome and brittle.
  • Minimizing Cognitive Overhead: Analysts spend up to 80% of their time cleaning data. A universal structural standard eliminates redundant custom-parsing scripts across different data ingestion pipelines.

1.3 Common Manifestations of Untidy Data

Real-world datasets typically violate tidy principles in five distinct ways:

  • Column headers are values, not variable names: For example, columns named 2021, 2022, and 2023 where the column name is actually the variable year.
  • Multiple variables are stored in a single column: For example, a column named rate containing entries like 120/80 (systolic/diastolic blood pressure) or US_urban (country_setting).
  • Variables are stored in both rows and columns: A layout where structural metadata and numeric measurements are interleaved across matrices.

Multiple types of observational units are stored in the same table: For instance, a table tracking song charts that simultaneously includes artist metadata (birth date, genre) and weekly chart rankings.

A single observational unit is stored across multiple tables: Fragmented data schemas that require complex joins or deep structural reshaping before analysis.

Part 2: Structural Transformation with tidyr

The tidyr package provides the programmatic verbs required to fix structural untidiness. While older R functions like reshape(), stack(), and unstack() existed, tidyr modernizes reshaping through unified, highly readable syntax.

2.1 Transitioning from Wide to Long: pivot_longer()

Datasets are frequently recorded in a wide format to optimize human data entry. For example, tracking a patient's cholesterol levels across four quarterly checkups creates four separate columns (q1, q2, q3, q4).

To analyze this longitudinally or plot trajectories over time using ggplot2, the data must be transformed into a long format using pivot_longer().

library(tidyverse)
# Create a messy wide dataset
patient_data_wide <- tibble( patient_id = c("P001", "P002", "P003"), gender = c("F", "M", "F"), q1_cholesterol = c(210, 190, 240), q2_cholesterol = c(205, 195, 230), q3_cholesterol = c(198, 185, 225) )
print(patient_data_wide)
To convert this dataset, we specify which columns to pivot, what to name the new key column (names_to), and what to name the new value column (values_to).
patient_data_long <- patient_data_wide %>%
  pivot_longer( cols = starts_with("q"), names_to = "quarter", values_to = "cholesterol_level" )
print(patient_data_long)
Advanced Options in pivot_longer()
  • names_prefix: Strips predictable prefixes (e.g., removing q_ or q from column names).
  • names_transform / values_transform: Apply functions (like as.integer or as.factor) directly during the pivoting process.
  • names_sep and names_to vectors: If a column name contains multiple variables encoded together (e.g., bp_q1_male), names_sep allows splitting that single column header into multiple distinct tidy columns simultaneously.
# Example with multi-variable column names
complex_wide <- tibble(
id = c(1, 2), mean_temp_2022 = c(15, 12), max_temp_2022 = c(25, 22), mean_temp_2023 = c(16, 13), max_temp_2023 = c(26, 23)
)
tidy_complex <- complex_wide %>%
  pivot_longer( cols = -id, names_to = c(".value", "year"), names_pattern = "(.*)_temp_(.*)"
)
print(tidy_complex)

2.2 Transitioning from Long to Wide: pivot_wider()

Conversely, data is sometimes excessively long—such as when multiple clinical metrics (heart rate, temperature, blood pressure) are stored as stacked rows under a single metric_name column, with their measurements in a single metric_value column.

clinical_long <- tibble( visit_id = c(101, 101, 102, 102), test_name = c("heart_rate", "temperature", "heart_rate", "temperature"),
test_result = c(72, 98.6, 80, 99.1)
)
print(clinical_long)

To reshape this into a wide format where each test has its own dedicated column:

clinical_wide <- clinical_long %>%
  pivot_wider(
names_from = test_name, values_from = test_result
)
print(clinical_wide)
Handling Aggregation Conflicts in pivot_wider()

If multiple rows map to the same cell intersection during pivot_wider(), tidyr throws an error because the resulting cell would require a list or vector. You can resolve this by passing aggregation functions (values_fn) or checking for duplicate identifier keys before pivoting. R

# Example handling duplicates safely duplicated_long <- tibble( patient = c("A", "A", "A"), visit = c(1, 1, 1), symptom = c("fever", "fever", "cough"), # Duplicate 'fever' entry

severity = c(2, 3, 1)

)

# Using values_fn to aggregate duplicates (e.g., taking the mean) resolved_wide <- duplicated_long %>%

pivot_wider(

names_from = symptom,

values_from = severity,

values_fn = mean )

Part 3: Advanced Data Tidying and Implicit Missingness

Tidying data frequently exposes structural gaps. Datasets often omit rows where observations did not occur or were never recorded, leading to implicit missing values.

3.1 Explicit vs. Implicit Missingness

  • Explicit Missingness (NA): The row and column exist, but the cell value is explicitly coded as missing (NA).
  • Implicit Missingness: The row itself is completely missing from the dataset. For example, if site #3 recorded no data in February, the row for February at site #3 might be entirely absent rather than present with an NA value.
# Implicit missingness example: Site 2 has no data for Feb
weather_data <- tibble( site = c("Site_1", "Site_1", "Site_2"),
month = c("Jan", "Feb", "Jan"), rainfall = c(45, 30, 50) )

3.2 Forcing Completeness with complete() and expand()

To perform accurate time-series modeling or spatial interpolation, implicit gaps must be made explicit. The complete() function generates all combinations of specified categorical variables and fills missing entries with NA or custom defaults.

complete_weather <- weather_data %>%
complete(site, month, fill = list(rainfall = 0))
print(complete_weather)

3.3 Filling Missing Values Down or Up (fill())

In panel datasets or longitudinal tracking sheets, values are frequently left blank in subsequent rows when they repeat from the row above (often for visual formatting in spreadsheets). The fill() function propagates previous non-missing values forward (downward) or backward (upward).

# Spreadsheet-style repeated values
survey_responses <- tibble( region = c("North", NA, NA, "South", NA), district = c("A", "B", "C", "A", "B"), score = c(85, 90, 78, 92, 88) )
# Filling missing region values downward
fixed_survey <- survey_responses %>%
  fill(region, .direction = "down")
print(fixed_survey)

3.4 Separating and Uniting Compound Columns (separate() and unite())

Tidy data requires each column to represent a single variable. When multiple variables are glued together inside a single column string (e.g., 2023-Q1 or NewYork_USA), separate() splits them.

raw_demographics <- tibble(
id = 1:3,
location_code = c("NYC_NY", "LAX_CA", "ORD_IL") )
tidy_demographics <- raw_demographics %>%
separate(
col = location_code, into = c("city", "state"), sep = "_" )
print(tidy_demographics)
Conversely, unite()
merges multiple columns into a single string column, which is useful for creating composite keys.
recombined_demographics <- tidy_demographics %>%
unite(
col = "full_location", city, state, sep = ", "
)
print(recombined_demographics)
Part 4: String Manipulation and Text Parsing with stringr

Numerical data requires mathematical transformations, but text data requires string manipulation. The stringr package provides a unified, consistent grammar for pattern matching, string modification, and regex operations in R. All functions begin with the prefix str_ and consistently place the string vector as their first argument,

making them fully compatible with the %>% pipe operator.

4.1 Core Characteristics of stringr

Consistent Argument Order: str_function(string, pattern, ...) ensures intuitive piping.

Vectorization: Every function automatically vectorizes over character vectors, eliminating the need for explicit sapply() or for loops.

Consistent Error Handling: Functions handle edge cases (like empty strings or missing inputs (NA)) predictably and safely.

4.2 Case Conversion and Whitespace Normalization

Real-world text strings often suffer from erratic capitalization and stray whitespace introduced by manual form inputs or web scraping. R

messy_strings <- c(" New York ", "los angeles", "SAN FRANCISCO ", "\tChicago\n")

# Normalize whitespace and capitalization

clean_strings <- messy_strings %>%

str_squish() %>% # Removes leading/trailing spaces and collapses internal whitespace

str_to_title() # Converts to Title Case

print(clean_strings) Key functions in this category include:

  • str_to_lower(): Converts all characters to lowercase.
  • str_to_upper(): Converts all characters to uppercase.
  • str_to_title(): Capitalizes the first letter of each word.
  • str_trim(): Strips whitespace exclusively from the edges (start and end).
  • str_squish(): Strips edge whitespace and replaces interior whitespace sequences with a single space.

4.3 Detecting, Locating, and Filtering Strings

Before transforming text, you often need to check whether specific patterns exist within your character vectors.

  • str_detect(): Returns a logical boolean vector (TRUE or FALSE) indicating whether a pattern matches. Excellent for filtering rows with dplyr::filter().
  • str_subset(): Returns only the elements of the character vector that match the pattern (equivalent to x[str_detect(x, pattern)]).
  • str_count(): Counts how many times a pattern appears within each string.
  • str_locate(): Returns the starting and ending character positions of the first match.
feedback_comments <- c(
"The product was fantastic and arrived early.",
"Terrible customer service. Completely unsatisfied.",
"It was okay, nothing special.",
"Fantastic quality, highly recommend!"
)
# Filter comments containing positive sentiment keywords
positive_feedback <- feedback_comments[str_detect(feedb ack_comments, regex("fantastic|recommend", ignore_case = TRUE))]
print(positive_feedback)

4.4 Extracting Substrings and Pattern Matches

When extracting specific segments from structured text (such as invoice numbers, postal codes, or embedded dates), extraction functions are indispensable.

str_sub(): Extracts text based on fixed integer character positions (start and end indexes).

str_extract() / str_extract_all(): Extracts the actual text matching a regular expression pattern.

invoice_codes <- c("INV-9821-US", "INV-4412-EU", "INV-0039-AP") # Extract only the numeric ID using regular expressions
numeric_ids <- str_extract(invoice_codes, "\\d{4}")
print(numeric_ids)

4.5 Replacing and Modifying Strings

Cleaning text often requires substituting erroneous characters, masking sensitive data, or reformatting codes.

  • str_replace(): Replaces the first occurrence of a pattern in each string.
  • str_replace_all(): Replaces all occurrences of a pattern in each string.

str_remove() / str_remove_all(): Convenience wrappers that replace matched patterns with empty strings.

phone_numbers <- c("555-019-2831", "555-492-1102", "(555) 883-9921") # Standardize phone formats by removing punctuation characters
standardized_phones <- phone_numbers %>%
str_remove_all("[\\-\\(\\)\\s]")
print(standardized_phones)
Part 5: Comprehensive End-to-End Practical Case Study

To cement these concepts, let us walk through a comprehensive datacleaning pipeline that combines tidyr structural reshaping, missing value remediation, and stringr text processing.

Scenario

Imagine you are a data analyst at a global retail enterprise. You have been handed an unpolished quarterly performance export (raw_sales_export) containing regional sales metrics. The file suffers from the following issues:

Sales figures are spread across wide month columns (m_jan, m_feb, m_mar).

Region and store codes are combined into a single messy column (store_code) separated by hyphens, complete with inconsistent capitalization and stray whitespace.

Revenue figures are stored as currency strings (e.g., "$1,250.00") rather than numeric values.

There are implicit missing gaps and explicit NA entries in customer satisfaction ratings.

Step-by-Step Implementation

library(tidyverse)
# 1. Simulate the Messy Raw Dataset
raw_sales_export <- tibble(
store_code = c(" us-east-01 ", "US-WEST-02", "eu-central-01", "EU-NORTH-02 "),
manager_name = c("Alice Smith", "Bob Jones", "Charlie Brown", "Diana Prince"),
m_jan = c("$1,200.50", "$950.00", "$1,400.00", NA),
m_feb = c("$1,350.25", "$1,100.00", "$1,250.00", "$800.00"),
m_mar = c("$1,500.00", "$1,250.50", "$1,600.00", "$920.00"),
satisfaction_score = c("4.5 / 5", " 3.8 / 5 ", NA, "4.2 / 5")
)
print("--- RAW DATASET ---")
print(raw_sales_export)
# 2. Comprehensive Cleaning Pipeline
tidy_sales_analytics <- raw_sales_export %>%
# Step A: Clean store code strings and separate into region and store number
mutate(
store_code = str_squish(str_to_lower(store_code) )
) %>%
  separate(
col = store_code,
into = c("region", "subregion", "store_id"), sep = "-" ) %>%
  # Unite region and subregion back for a clean regional identifier
unite( col = "region",
region, subregion, sep = "_"
# ) %>%
# Step B: Clean satisfaction score by extracting the numeric rating and converting to double
mutate(
satisfaction_score = str_remove(satisfaction_score, "/ 5"),
satisfaction_score = str_trim(satisfaction_score),
satisfaction_score = as.numeric(satisfaction_score)
) %>%
# Step C: Reshape wide monthly sales columns to long format
pivot_longer(
cols = starts_with("m_"),
names_to = "month", values_to = "revenue_str"
) %>%
# Step D: Clean monthly sales revenue strings (remove dollar signs and commas) and convert to numeric
mutate(
month = str_remove(month, "m_"), month = str_to_title(month),
revenue_str = str_remove_all(revenue_str, "[\\$,]"),
revenue = as.numeric(revenue_str)
) %>%
select(-revenue_str) %>%
  # Drop intermediate string column
# Step E: Handle missing values gracefully
replace_na(list(revenue = 0.0, satisfaction_score = median(.$satisfaction_score, na.rm = TRUE)))
print("--- FULLY CLEANED & TIDY DATASET ---")
print(tidy_sales_analytics)
Analysis of Pipeline Steps

String Sanitization (str_squish, str_to_lower): Standardizes chaotic entry variations like "

us-east-01 " into predictable lowercase tokens.

Structural Splitting (separate, unite): Deconstructs compound identifiers into discrete tidy analytical variables (region, store_id).

Regex Extraction & Type Casting (str_remove, as.numeric): Strips currency symbols ($), thousands separators (,), and rating denominator labels (/ 5) before casting raw text into mathematically operable floatingpoint vectors.

  • Reshaping (pivot_longer): Converts wide monthly columns into a clean time-series observation schema.
  • Missing Value Imputation (replace_na): Replaces unrecorded revenue values with zero and imputes missing satisfaction scores using the statistical median.

Part 6: Summary Checklist for Module Mastery

  • ☐ Understand Tidy Rules: Can you verify whether a given dataset violates any of Wickham's three tidy principles?
  • ☐ Reshape Data Fluently: Can you write pivot_longer() and pivot_wider() statements with custom argument configurations (names_prefix, values_fn)?
  • ☐ Handle Implicit and Explicit Missingness: Do you know when to apply complete(), fill(), and replace_na()?
  • ☐ Master Text Processing with stringr: Can you combine regular expressions, case conversion, whitespace normalization, and string extraction in a dplyr pipeline?

quiz.q: Which function reshapes data from wide to long?
quiz.e: pivot_longer() gathers columns into name/value pairs.

quiz.q: Which function reshapes data from long to wide?
quiz.e: pivot_wider() spreads names into columns.

quiz.q: What does complete() do in tidyr?
quiz.e: complete() fills in missing combinations of values.

quiz.q: What does fill() do?
o: Replaces NA values by carrying neighbouring values down or up
quiz.e: fill() propagates values down or up over NAs.

quiz.q: Which pair splits one column into several and joins several into one?
quiz.e: separate() splits compound columns; unite() merges them.

quiz.q: Which stringr function trims leading/trailing spaces and collapses internal whitespace?
quiz.e: str_squish() normalizes whitespace.

quiz.q: Which function tests whether a pattern is present in each string?
quiz.e: str_detect() returns a logical vector.

quiz.q: What do stringr functions share by design?
o: They all begin with str_ and take the string as the first argument
quiz.e: Consistent str_ prefix and string-first arguments make them pipe-friendly.
